demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Triggers.value: Beginning to feel detached or unreal
Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
I should have protected others and I failed

issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: 'Talks or photos about snakes' is not clinically coherent as a trigger for PTSD centered on the unexpected death of a loved one unless the death involved snakes, which is not indicated. It appears trauma-unrelated and weakly connected to the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: 'I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened' implies perceived preventability and personal responsibility during the death event. That can occur, but it is not supported by the rest of the profile, which lacks any memory or trigger content suggesting direct involvement in the loved one's death.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid New Relationships: Starting new friendships or relationships
issues.explanation: 'Starting new friendships or relationships' as an avoided strategy is a poor fit for a married 28-year-old male whose trauma is bereavement, and it is not well linked to the stated triggers/appraisals. It suggests interpersonal avoidance without supporting appraisals such as mistrust, fear of loss, or social threat.

vignette: Carlos Hernandez still remembers the exact date his younger brother, Juan, was shot in a drive-by shooting outside their family's restaurant. It was a typical Friday evening in April 2018. Carlos had just finished a long shift as a prison guard and was heading home when he received the devastating call from his sister-in-law. The image of Juan's lifeless body on the pavement is forever etched in his mind. In the months that followed, Carlos struggled to come to terms with the loss. He would often find himself zoning out, feeling detached from his surroundings as if observing his own life from afar. These dissociative episodes were particularly distressing when triggered by news reports of similar violent incidents or conversations about people losing loved ones. The mere mention of such topics would send Carlos's mind racing back to that fateful night. To cope with the emotional pain, Carlos started engaging in maladaptive strategies. He would cover his face with his hands whenever memories of Juan resurfaced, as if hiding from the world could shield him from the grief. At home, he began picking arguments with his wife, Sarah, creating unnecessary drama to distract himself from the trauma. Their relationship became increasingly strained, and they started attending couples therapy in an attempt to salvage their bond. However, the most pervasive coping mechanism Carlos developed was avoidance. He steered clear of anything that reminded him of Juan - no more visiting their family's restaurant, no more looking at old photos, no more listening to music they used to share. This avoidance behavior extended to his occupation as a prison guard; he started requesting transfers to different units, hoping to escape the constant reminders of violence and loss. As time passed, Carlos became increasingly convinced that he had lost his former self - the happy-go-lucky person who always wore a smile on his face. He felt hopeless about the future, convinced that he would never find joy again. What's more, the weight of responsibility for Juan's death continued to haunt him; Carlos couldn't shake off the feeling that he should have been there to protect his brother. These negative appraisals took a toll on Carlos's daily life. He started questioning the purpose of his job as a prison guard, wondering if it was worth the emotional burden. His relationship with Sarah suffered further, and their social life dwindled to almost nothing. Friends and family grew concerned about Carlos's withdrawal from social activities. It wasn't until Carlos had a particularly distressing dissociative episode during a routine patrol at work that he realized he needed help. As he stood frozen, feeling like an outsider in his own body, he knew he couldn't continue living this way. With Sarah's encouragement, Carlos finally sought professional help, hoping to break free from the shackles of grief and find a way back to the person he used to be. As Carlos begins therapy, he's most afraid of confronting the emotions he's been trying to suppress for so long. What if he loses control? What if he can't bear the pain? But, deep down, he also hopes that this journey will allow him to rediscover his sense of purpose and find a way to heal - not just for himself, but for Juan's memory as well.
